claim: CHK2 is a critical negative regulator of androgen receptor (AR) transcriptional activity, prostate cancer (PCa) cell growth, and androgen sensitivity.
source: We have previously demonstrated that checkpoint kinase 2 (CHK2) is a critical negative regulator of androgen receptor (AR) transcriptional activity, prostate cancer (PCa) cell growth, and androgen sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The AR directly interacts with CHK2.
source: We have now uncovered that the AR directly interacts with CHK2
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Far western blotting experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ionizing radiation (IR) increases the AR-CHK2 interaction.
source: We have now uncovered that the AR directly interacts with CHK2 and ionizing radiation (IR) increases this interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: PCa associated CHK2 mutants with impaired kinase activity reduced IR-induced AR-CHK2 interactions.
source: PCa associated CHK2 mutants with impaired kinase activity reduced IR-induced AR–CHK2 interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating reduced AR-CHK2 association with K373E and T387N mutants after IR.

claim: The destabilization of AR-CHK2 interactions induced by CHK2 variants impairs CHK2 negative regulation of cell growth.
source: The destabilization of AR – CHK2 interactions induced by CHK2 variants impairs CHK2 negative regulation of cell growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 demonstrating that CHK2 mutants K373E and T387N have reduced ability to suppress cell growth compared to wtCHK2.

claim: CHK2 depletion increases transcription of DNAPK.
source: CHK2 depletion increases transcription of DNAPK and RAD54
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CHK2 depletion increases transcription of RAD54.
source: CHK2 depletion increases transcription of DNAPK and RAD54
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CHK2 depletion increases clonogenic survival following ionizing radiation.
source: CHK2 depletion increases transcription of DNAPK and RAD54, increases clonogenic survival
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic survival assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CHK2 depletion increases resolution of DNA double strand breaks.
source: CHK2 depletion increases transcription of DNAPK and RAD54, increases clonogenic survival, and increases resolution of DNA double strand breaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by comet assay data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating less DNA breaks at 24 hr with CHK2 knockdown.

claim: CHK2 sequesters the AR through direct binding decreasing AR transcription and suppressing PCa cell growth.
source: The data support a model where CHK2 sequesters the AR through direct binding decreasing AR transcription and suppressing PCa cell growth.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including direct binding data (Figure 1), transcription data (Figure 4), and cell growth data (Figure 3).

claim: CHK2 mutation or loss of expression leads to increased AR transcriptional activity and survival in response to DNA damage.
source: CHK2 mutation or loss of expression thereby leads to increased AR transcriptional activity and survival in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing increased transcription of DDR genes (Figure 4) and increased clonogenic survival (Figure 5A) with CHK2 knockdown.

claim: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains one of the leading causes of death among men of all races.
source: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains one of the leading causes of death among men of all races (cdc.gov)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to CDC data.

claim: Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is currently incurable.
source: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains one of the leading causes of death among men of all races (cdc.gov), as castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is currently incurable.
evidence: This claim is based on established medical knowledge about CRPC.

claim: The androgen receptor (AR) modulates the transcription of DDR genes and DNA repair.
source: Recently, the DDR has been a focus of PCa research since the androgen receptor (AR), a major driver of PCa, modulates the transcription of DDR genes and DNA repair (Polkinghorn et al., 2013; Goodwin et al., 2013; Jividen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CHK2 negatively regulates androgen sensitivity and PCa cell growth.
source: We have previously shown that checkpoint kinase 2 (CHK2) negatively regulates androgen sensitivity and PCa cell growth (Ta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: CHK2 is a serine/threonine protein kinase that plays a crucial role in sensing DNA damage and initiating the DDR.
source: CHK2 is a serine/threonine protein kinase that plays a crucial role in sensing DNA damage and initiating the DDR, which is comprised of cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis (Matsuoka et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about CHK2.

claim: CHK2 has a carboxy-terminal kinase domain (KD) and nuclear localization sequence.
source: a carboxy-terminal kinase domain (KD) and nuclear localization sequence Ahn et al., 2004
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about CHK2 structure.

claim: CHK2 has a central forkhead-associated domain (FHA) that provides an interface for interactions with phosphorylated proteins.
source: and a central forkhead-associated domain (FHA) that provides an interface for interactions with phosphorylated proteins (Li et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about CHK2 structure and function.

claim: There are approximately 24 CHK2 substrates in human cells that have been experimentally validated.
source: Currently, there are approximately 24 CHK2 substrates in human cells that have been experimentally validated, including polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1), promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML), E2F1, p53, and cell division cycle 25C (CDC25C) (García-Limones et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHK2 association with PLK1 leads to its localization at centrosomes where it regulates mitotic entry.
source: CHK2 association with PLK1 leads to its localization at centrosomes where it regulates mitotic entry (Tsvetkov et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHK2 autophosphorylation and activation are regulated by the tumor suppressor PML within nuclear matrix-associated structures called PML-nuclear bodies.
source: CHK2 autophosphorylation and activation are regulated by the tumor suppressor PML within nuclear matrix-associated structures called PML-nuclear bodies, which are nuclear matrix-associated structures (Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Binding to PML keeps CHK2 in an inactive state within PML-nuclear bodies.
source: Binding to PML keeps CHK2 in an inactive state within these PML-nuclear bodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Yang et al., 2002).

claim: Activated CHK2 can phosphorylate PML on S117 and induce PML-mediated apoptosis.
source: In return, activated CHK2 can phosphorylate PML on S117 and induce PML-mediated apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Yang et al., 2002).

claim: CHK2 can modify the transcription of apoptotic genes through direct binding and S364 phosphorylation of the E2F1 transcription factor in response to DNA damage.
source: CHK2 can also modify the transcription of apoptotic genes through direct binding and S364 phosphorylation of the E2F1 transcription factor in response to DNA damage, thereby stabilizing E2F1 and activating gene transcription (Stevens et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHK2 regulates apoptosis through p53 phosphorylation and promotion of p53-mediated cell death.
source: CHK2 also regulates apoptosis through p53 phosphorylation, and promotion of p53-mediated cell death (Hirao et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The interaction with the core domain of p53 induces an allosteric change in CHK2 which permits p53 S20 phosphorylation.
source: The interaction with the core domain of p53 induces an allosteric change in CHK2 which permits p53 S20 phosphorylation (Bartek and Lukas, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHK2 modulates CDC25C localization by associating with and phosphorylating CDC25 on S216, which creates a binding site for 14-3-3 proteins.
source: Moreover, CHK2 modulates CDC25C localization by associating with and phosphorylating CDC25 on S216, which creates a binding site for 14-3-3 proteins (Peng et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins sequester CDC25C in the cytoplasm and block the G2/M transition since cyclin dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) cannot be activated.
source: 14-3-3 proteins in turn sequester CDC25C in the cytoplasm and block the G2/M transition since cyclin dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) cannot be activated.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the CDC25C-14-3-3 interaction and cell cycle regulation.

claim: CHK2 co-immunoprecipitated with AR in PCa cells.
source: Finally, our group has shown that CHK2 co-immunoprecipitated with AR in PCa cells and regulated growth, suggesting that AR may be a novel substrate of CHK2 (Ta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: V5-wtCHK2 bound to FLAG-wtAR.
source: We found that V5-wtCHK2 bound to FLAG-wtAR, as well as the control FLAG-ERK2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Far western blotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: V5-wtCHK2 bound to FLAG-ERK2.
source: We found that V5-wtCHK2 bound to FLAG-wtAR, as well as the control FLAG-ERK2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Far western blotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AR S308A showed a statistically significant reduction in binding to CHK2 (adjusted p=0.035).
source: Only AR S308A showed a statistically significant reduction in binding to CHK2 (adjusted p=0.035), although all AR phosphorylation mutants trended to decrease association with CHK2.
evidence: This claim is supported by Far western blotting data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All AR phosphorylation mutants trended to decrease association with CHK2.
source: Only AR S308A showed a statistically significant reduction in binding to CHK2 (adjusted p=0.035), although all AR phosphorylation mutants trended to decrease association with CHK2.
evidence: This claim is supported by Far western blotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AR and CHK2 directly bind as shown by reciprocal Far western.
source: We observed the reciprocal binding of AR and CHK2 by Far western.
evidence: This claim is supported by Far western blotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reduced AR-CHK2 binding (adj p=0.026) was observed with the CHK2 K373E mutant.
source: We observed reduced AR – CHK2 binding (adj p=0.026) with the CHK2 K373E mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by Far western blotting data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No significant change in AR-CHK2 binding was observed with the CHK2 T387N mutant.
source: No significant change was observed with the CHK2 T387N mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by Far western blotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: AR phosphorylation and CHK2 kinase activity may impact AR-CHK2 binding.
source: These data suggest that the AR directly binds CHK2 and that AR phosphorylation and CHK2 kinase activity may impact that binding.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the Far western data showing effects of AR phosphorylation mutants and CHK2 kinase mutants on binding.

claim: There was a 4-fold increase in AR co-immunoprecipitating with CHK2 after IR treatment of cells expressing wtAR.
source: There was a 4-fold increase in AR co-immunoprecipitating with CHK2 after IR treatment of cells expressing wtAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neither S81A nor S308A increased in association with CHK2 upon IR treatment.
source: However, neither S81A nor S308A increased in association with CHK2 upon IR treatment indicating that phosphorylation of AR on S81 and S308 is required for the IR-induced increase in the interaction between AR and CHK2.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation of AR on S81 and S308 is required for the IR-induced increase in the interaction between AR and CHK2.
source: However, neither S81A nor S308A increased in association with CHK2 upon IR treatment indicating that phosphorylation of AR on S81 and S308 is required for the IR-induced increase in the interaction between AR and CHK2.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on co-immunoprecipitation data showing that AR phosphorylation mutants do not show IR-induced increase in CHK2 binding (Figure 2A).

claim: The basal level of CHK2 and AR co-immunoprecipitation was unaffected by AR phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to the AR – CHK2 association by Far western, the basal level of CHK2 and AR co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) was unaffected by AR phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There were no significant changes in S81 or S308 phosphorylation in response to IR in LNCaP or C4-2 cell lines.
source: There were no significant changes in S81 or S308 phosphorylation in response to IR in either cell line.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: While the intensity of S81 and S308 phosphorylation does not markedly change with IR, S81 and S308 phosphorylation is necessary for AR-CHK2 interactions under certain conditions.
source: Thus, these findings indicate that while the intensity of S81 and S308 phosphorylation does not markedly change with IR, S81 and S308 phosphorylation is necessary for AR – CHK2 interactions under certain conditions.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on data showing that AR phosphorylation mutants do not show IR-induced increase in CHK2 binding (Figure 2A) but phosphorylation levels do not change with IR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: In response to IR there was a striking increase in CHK2-AR co-association in cells expressing FLAG-wtCHK2 and HA-wtAR.
source: In response to IR there was a striking increase in CHK2 – AR co-association in cells expressing FLAG-wtCHK2 and HA-wtAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The amount of IR-induced increase in the AR-CHK2 association in cells expressing either K373E or T387N was dramatically reduced.
source: However, the amount of IR-induced increase in the AR – CHK2 association in cells expressing either K373E or T387N was dramatically reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No change in basal AR-CHK2 co-IP was observed with CHK2 mutants.
source: No change in basal AR – CHK2 co-IP was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The kinase activity of CHK2 is required for the optimal induction of the CHK2 and AR interaction in response to IR.
source: These data indicate that the kinase activity of CHK2 is required for the optimal induction of the CHK2 and AR interaction in response to IR, and that the CHK2 mutants associated with PCa have a diminished ability to interact with the AR in irradiated cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on co-immunoprecipitation data showing reduced IR-induced AR-CHK2 association with kinase-deficient CHK2 mutants (Figure 2B).

claim: The CHK2 mutants associated with PCa have a diminished ability to interact with the AR in irradiated cells.
source: These data indicate that the kinase activity of CHK2 is required for the optimal induction of the CHK2 and AR interaction in response to IR, and that the CHK2 mutants associated with PCa have a diminished ability to interact with the AR in irradiated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing reduced IR-induced AR-CHK2 association with PCa-associated CHK2 mutants K373E and T387N (Figure 2B).

claim: Knockdown of CHK2 significantly augmented growth in all PCa cell lines tested.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Ta et al., 2015), hormone stimulated growth of vector-expressing cells and knockdown of CHK2 significantly augmented growth in all PCa cell lines tested (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT cell growth assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Re-expression of wtCHK2, K373E, and T387N in CHK2-depleted cells markedly suppressed the increase in growth induced by CHK2 knockdown in all PCa cell lines tested.
source: Re-expression of wtCHK2, K373E, and T387N in CHK2-depleted cells markedly suppressed the increase in growth induced by CHK2 knockdown in all PCa cell lines tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT cell growth assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In LNCaP cells the extent of growth inhibition induced by K373E and T387N was significantly less than that generated by wtCHK2.
source: Interestingly, in LNCaP cells the extent of growth inhibition induced by K373E and T387N was significantly less than that generated by wtCHK2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT cell growth assay data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The effect of CHK2 re-expression on cell growth in castration-resistant C4-2 and Rv1 cells was not significantly different between wtCHK2 and the kinase deficient K373E and T387N mutants.
source: The effect of CHK2 re-expression on cell growth in castration-resistant C4-2 (Figure 3B) and Rv1 (Figure 3C) cells was not significantly different between wtCHK2 and the kinase deficient K373E and T387N mutants, although the magnitude of inhibition caused by the mutants was consistently less than that produced by wtCHK2.
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT cell growth assay data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The magnitude of inhibition caused by K373E and T387N mutants was consistently less than that produced by wtCHK2 in C4-2 and Rv1 cells.
source: The effect of CHK2 re-expression on cell growth in castration-resistant C4-2 (Figure 3B) and Rv1 (Figure 3C) cells was not significantly different between wtCHK2 and the kinase deficient K373E and T387N mutants, although the magnitude of inhibition caused by the mutants was consistently less than that produced by wtCHK2.
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT cell growth assay data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: CHK2 kinase activity limits the ability of CHK2 to negatively regulate PCa cell growth, especially in androgen dependent PCa.
source: These observations suggest that CHK2 kinase activity limits the ability of CHK2 to negatively regulate PCa cell growth, especially in androgen dependent PCa.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on cell growth data showing differential effects of CHK2 mutants in androgen-dependent vs castration-resistant cell lines (Figure 3).

claim: Knockdown of CHK2 in LNCaP cells grown in CSS and stimulated with 1 nM DHT led to an increase in transcription of DNAPK and RAD54 in response to IR.
source: Knockdown of CHK2 in LNCaP cells grown in CSS and stimulated with 1 nM DHT led to an increase in transcription of DNAPK and RAD54 in response to IR, suggesting that CHK2 may suppress AR transcription of DDR genes in response to IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CHK2 may suppress AR transcription of DDR genes in response to IR.
source: Knockdown of CHK2 in LNCaP cells grown in CSS and stimulated with 1 nM DHT led to an increase in transcription of DNAPK and RAD54 in response to IR, suggesting that CHK2 may suppress AR transcription of DDR genes in response to IR.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on qPCR data showing increased DDR gene transcription with CHK2 knockdown (Figure 4).

claim: CHK2 knockdown promoted cell survival following ionizing radiation.
source: Clonogenic assays revealed that CHK2 knockdown promoted cell survival following ionizing radiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic survival assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of CHK2 could facilitate DNA repair.
source: This data, along with the data above indicating that CHK2 suppresses AR transcription of DNA repair genes suggested the hypothesis that loss of CHK2 could facilitate DNA repair.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on data showing increased survival (Figure 5A) and increased DDR gene transcription (Figure 4) with CHK2 knockdown.

claim: Statistically significant less DNA breaks were observed with CHK2 knockdown at 24 hr in LNCaP cells.
source: When we examined DNA damage using the comet assay, we observed statistically significant less DNA breaks with CHK2 knockdown at 24 hr in LNCaP cells (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comet assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The comet assay shows less % DNA in tail, shorter DNA tail length, and lower tail moment with CHK2 knockdown suggesting more efficient DNA repair when CHK2 is compromised.
source: The comet assay shows less % DNA in tail, shorter DNA tail length, and lower tail moment with CHK2 knockdown suggesting more efficient DNA repair when CHK2 is compromised.
evidence: This claim is supported by comet assay data shown in Figure 5B and is an inference about DNA repair efficiency.

claim: Radiation induced more γH2AX foci at 15 min when CHK2 was knocked down.
source: Radiation induced more γH2AX foci at 15 min when CHK2 was knocked down (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Less γH2AX foci are found in CHK2 knock-down cells at 2 hr.
source: However, less foci are found in CHK2 knock-down cells at 2 hr and by 4 hr through 24 hr an equal number of foci are present in control and CHK2 knock-down cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: By 4 hr through 24 hr an equal number of γH2AX foci are present in control and CHK2 knock-down cells.
source: However, less foci are found in CHK2 knock-down cells at 2 hr and by 4 hr through 24 hr an equal number of foci are present in control and CHK2 knock-down cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H2AX is phosphorylated in response to inputs in addition to IR induced DNA double strand breaks, including RNA polymerase II dependent transcription.
source: H2AX is phosphorylated in response to inputs in addition to IR induced DNA double strand breaks, including RNA polymerase II dependent transcription (Singh et al., 2015; Bunch et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: No significant differences in 53BP1 foci were found when CHK2 was knocked down.
source: Therefore, we also measured 53BP1 foci to assess DSB repair and found no significant differences when CHK2 was knocked down (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The apparent discrepancy in the 53BP1 and γH2AX foci may be explained by an increase in transcription when CHK2 is knocked down.
source: The apparent discrepancy in the 53BP1 and γH2AX foci may be explained by an increase in transcription when CHK2 is knocked down, as shown in Figure 4 and in our previous study (Ta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the discrepancy between γH2AX and 53BP1 data, based on previous findings about CHK2 effects on transcription.

claim: CHK2 acts as a tumor suppressor in PCa, either through loss of expression or mutation.
source: The data reported herein along with our previous work (Ta et al., 2015) indicate that CHK2 acts as a tumor suppressor in PCa, either through loss of expression or mutation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript showing that CHK2 loss or mutation increases cell growth and survival.

claim: CHK2 antagonists in clinical development may paradoxically lead to enhanced PCa growth and resistance to IR.
source: This raises the concern that CHK2 antagonists in clinical development may paradoxically lead to enhanced PCa growth and resistance to IR.
evidence: This is a speculation about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition is different than inhibition by RNAi.
source: It is important to consider that pharmacologic inhibition is different than inhibition by RNAi (Jensen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Wild-type CHK2 maintains homeostasis through mediating the balance between DNA repair and cell death.
source: Wild-type CHK2 maintains homeostasis through mediating the balance between DNA repair and cell death, antagonizes the AR through direct binding and inhibition of transcription of AR target genes while AR transcriptionally represses CHK2.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CHK2 antagonizes the AR through direct binding and inhibition of transcription of AR target genes.
source: Wild-type CHK2 maintains homeostasis through mediating the balance between DNA repair and cell death, antagonizes the AR through direct binding and inhibition of transcription of AR target genes while AR transcriptionally represses CHK2.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data showing direct AR-CHK2 binding (Figure 1) and CHK2 suppression of AR target gene transcription (Figure 4).

claim: AR transcriptionally represses CHK2.
source: Wild-type CHK2 maintains homeostasis through mediating the balance between DNA repair and cell death, antagonizes the AR through direct binding and inhibition of transcription of AR target genes while AR transcriptionally represses CHK2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Ta et al., 2015).

claim: This feedback loop enables AR repression of CHK2 to turn off the DDR, while CHK2 negatively regulates AR to dampen growth during repair of damaged DNA.
source: This feedback loop enables AR repression of CHK2 to turn off the DDR, while CHK2 negatively regulates AR to dampen growth during repair of damaged DNA.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data and represents an inference about the functional significance of the AR-CHK2 interaction.

claim: CHK2 mutation or loss of expression in PCa leads to increased AR transcriptional activity, possibly of DDR genes, and survival in response to DNA damage, all leading to a more aggressive cancer.
source: CHK2 mutation or loss of expression in PCa leads to increased AR transcriptional activity, possibly of DDR genes, and survival in response to DNA damage, all leading to a more aggressive cancer.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data showing increased DDR gene transcription (Figure 4), increased survival (Figure 5A), and effects of CHK2 mutants (Figures 2, 3).

claim: The K373E CHK2 mutation impairs CHK2 function suppressing cell growth and promoting survival in response to IR, as a result of reduced kinase activity due to the disruption of CHK2 autophosphorylation.
source: The K373E CHK2 mutation impairs CHK2 function suppressing cell growth and promoting survival in response to IR, as a result of reduced kinase activity due to the disruption of CHK2 autophosphorylation (Higashiguchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The T387N CHK2 mutation is reported to diminish kinase activity.
source: Less is known about the heterozygous missense mutation T387N, but it is reported to diminish kinase activity (Wasielewski et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHK2 physically associates with ERK1/2 in cancer cells.
source: We used FLAG-ERK2 as a positive control since it has been reported that CHK2 physically associates with ERK1/2 in cancer cells (Dai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A significant increase in CHK2-ERK association was observed with IR.
source: Interestingly, we observed a significant increase in CHK2–ERK association with IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Far western experiments (implied from the text discussing ERK as a positive control).

claim: IR increases CHK2 T68 phosphorylation, which is required for the CHK2-ERK interaction.
source: This is consistent with IR increasing CHK2 T68 phosphorylation, which is required for the CHK2–ERK interaction.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on established knowledge about CHK2 T68 phosphorylation and the observed increase in CHK2-ERK association with IR.

claim: CHK2 has been implicated in diverse cellular processes.
source: These data point to a potentially larger role for CHK2 beyond canonical DDR and cell cycle checkpoint signaling; consistent with this notion CHK2 has been implicated in diverse cellular processes (Zannini et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2014; Choudhuri et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MEK inhibition is effective in lung tumors with ATM mutations where CHK2 is inactive.
source: MEK inhibition is effective in lung tumors with ATM mutations where CHK2 is inactive (Smida et al., 2016) providing further support that CHK2 negatively regulates ERK.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHK2 may serve as a general negative regulator of mitogenic signals in response to IR.
source: Negative regulation of both the AR and ERK by CHK2 suggests the hypothesis that CHK2 may serve as a general negative regulator of mitogenic signals in response to IR.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing CHK2 negative regulation of both AR and ERK.

claim: Androgen and IR increased DNAPK, XRCC2, and XRCC3 according to reports by others.
source: Reports by others demonstrate that androgen and IR increased DNAPK, XRCC2, and XRCC3 (Goodwin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The discrepancy in the DDR gene subsets regulated by the AR in different studies may be system dependent.
source: The discrepancy in the DDR gene subsets regulated by the AR in these studies and ours may be system dependent.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain differences between studies.

claim: CHK2 binding to the AR suppresses AR transcription of DDR genes enabling cells to turn off the DDR following DNA repair.
source: However, it also indicates that the dogma of AR regulating DDR genes needs further examination. Our data indicate that CHK2 knockdown increases DNAPK and RAD54 transcript levels is consistent with our earlier observation that CHK2 knockdown led to the increase in the transcripts of canonical AR target genes (Ta et al., 2015). This leads to the hypothesis that CHK2 binding to the AR suppresses AR transcription of DDR genes enabling cells to turn off the DDR following DNA repair.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing increased DDR gene transcription with CHK2 knockdown (Figure 4).

claim: PARP-1 was recruited to AR binding sites, enhancing AR occupancy and transcriptional function.
source: PARP-1 was recruited to AR binding sites, enhancing AR occupancy and transcriptional function (Schiewer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tandem mass spectroscopy analysis identified Ku70 and Ku80 as direct AR-interacting proteins that positively regulate AR transactivation.
source: Tandem mass spectroscopy analysis identified Ku70 and Ku80 as direct AR-interacting proteins that positively regulate AR transactivation (Mayeur et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: BRCA1 physically interacted with the DNA-binding domain (DBD) of AR to enhance AR transactivation and induce androgen-mediated cell death through p21 expression.
source: Furthermore, BRCA1 physically interacted with the DNA-binding domain (DBD) of AR to enhance AR transactivation and induce androgen-mediated cell death through p21 expression (Yeh et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The association of the LBD of AR with hRad9 suppressed AR transactivation by preventing the androgen-induced interaction between the n-terminus and c-terminus of AR.
source: In contrast, the association of the LBD of AR with hRad9, a crucial member of the checkpoint Rad family, suppressed AR transactivation by preventing the androgen-induced interaction between the n-terminus and c-terminus of AR (Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mediator of DNA damage checkpoint protein 1 (MDC1) physically associated with FL-AR and ARV7 to negatively regulate PCa cell growth and migration.
source: Mediator of DNA damage checkpoint protein 1 (MDC1), an essential player in the Intra-S phase and G2/M checkpoints, physically associated with FL-AR and ARV7 to negatively regulate PCa cell growth and migration (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Increased clonogenic survival following IR was a consequence of DNA-PKc directly complexing with both FL-AR and ARV5-7, with radiation increasing these interactions and enzalutamide blocking the association with FL-AR but not ARV5-7.
source: Yin and colleagues, on the other hand, showed that increased clonogenic survival following IR was a consequence of DNA-PKc directly complexing with both FL-AR and ARV5-7, with radiation increasing these interactions and enzalutamide blocking the association with FL-AR but not ARV5-7 (Yin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AR is integrated in the DDR, interfacing at multiple points.
source: These data support a model where AR is integrated in the DDR, interfacing at multiple points.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature cited showing multiple DDR protein-AR interactions.

claim: AR interacts with CHK2 through the CHK2 FHA domain.
source: Since proteins containing FHA domains bind phosphoproteins (Li et al., 2002), we hypothesize that AR interacts with CHK2 through the CHK2 FHA domain.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge about FHA domains and the data showing AR phosphorylation is required for binding.

claim: AR physically associated with the FHA domain of MDC1.
source: In support of this, the Zhao lab determined that AR physically associated with the FHA domain of another critical DDR member, MDC1 (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AR only co-immunoprecipitated with MDC1 mutants containing the FHA domain in the absence and presence of dihydrotestosterone.
source: Expression of truncation mutants of different MDC1 domains in LNCaP cells led to the discovery that AR only co-immunoprecipitated with MDC1 mutants containing the FHA domain in the absence and presence of dihydrotestosterone.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2015).

claim: The FHA domain of MDC1 mediated the interaction with AR.
source: Their results indicated that the FHA domain of MDC1 mediated the interaction with AR.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2015).

claim: AR S81 and S308 can both be phosphorylated by CDK1.
source: AR S81 and S308 can both be phosphorylated by CDK1, which is downstream of canonical CHK2 signaling (Chen et al., 2012; Koryakina et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S81 is predominantly phosphorylated by CDK9.
source: However, our previous studies demonstrated that S81 is predominantly phosphorylated by CDK9, and thus is more indicative of AR transcriptional activity (Gordon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: S308 phosphorylation was restricted to late G2 and M phase of the cell cycle.
source: We also found that S308 phosphorylation was restricted to late G2 and M phase of the cell cycle (Koryakina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The hormone induced activation state of the AR is a critical determinant in the IR induced increase in AR-CHK2 association.
source: The disconnect between these sites being required for the IR induced increase in AR – CHK2 association but not being regulated by IR suggests that the hormone induced activation state of the AR is a critical determinant in the IR induced increase in AR – CHK2 association.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing AR phosphorylation is required for IR-induced AR-CHK2 association but phosphorylation levels don't change with IR.

claim: Additional proteins present in cells may assist and participate in the AR-CHK2 interaction.
source: This suggests that additional proteins present in cells may assist and participate in the AR – CHK2 interaction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on differences observed between Far western and co-IP experiments.

claim: The fold change in growth suppression between wtCHK2 and CHK2 variants was greater in androgen-dependent LNCaP cells than in castration-resistant C4-2 and Rv1 cells.
source: Moreover, the fold change in growth suppression between wtCHK2 and CHK2 variants was greater in androgen-dependent LNCaP cells than in castration-resistant C4-2 and Rv1 cells, suggesting that in hormone sensitive PCa CHK2 variants may play a larger role in regulating growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell growth data shown in Figure 3 and represents an inference about the differential effects in different cell types.

claim: In hormone sensitive PCa CHK2 variants may play a larger role in regulating growth.
source: Moreover, the fold change in growth suppression between wtCHK2 and CHK2 variants was greater in androgen-dependent LNCaP cells than in castration-resistant C4-2 and Rv1 cells, suggesting that in hormone sensitive PCa CHK2 variants may play a larger role in regulating growth.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential effects of CHK2 mutants in different cell types (Figure 3).

claim: The CHK2 mutants found in PCa with diminished AR binding may be selected for, decreasing CHK2 suppression of AR activity and PCa cell growth.
source: This raises the possibility that the CHK2 mutants found in PCa with diminished AR binding are selected for, decreasing CHK2 suppression of AR activity and PCa cell growth.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary selection of CHK2 mutants in PCa.

claim: Numerous CHK2 splice variants were discovered in breast cancer tissue, where all variants were co-expressed with wtCHK2.
source: Berge and colleagues discovered numerous CHK2 splice variants in breast cancer tissue, where all variants were co-expressed with wtCHK2 (Berge et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Several CHK2 variants reduced kinase activity when simultaneously expressed with wtCHK2 and displayed a dominant negative effect on wtCHK2.
source: Furthermore, several of these variants reduced kinase activity when simultaneously expressed with wtCHK2 and displayed a dominant negative effect on wtCHK2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Berge et al., 2010).

claim: CHK2 negatively regulates ERK.
source: MEK inhibition is effective in lung tumors with ATM mutations where CHK2 is inactive (Smida et al., 2016) providing further support that CHK2 negatively regulates ERK.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing increased CHK2-ERK association with IR and literature showing MEK inhibition is effective when CHK2 is inactive.

claim: Approximately 88 men die from PCa every day.
source: PCa is the most frequently diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death among American men, with approximately 88 men dying from PCa every day (pcf.org).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to data from pcf.org.

claim: PARP inhibitors may be efficacious in CRPC patients with mutations in DDR genes.
source: Recently, there has been an emphasis on understanding the link between the DDR and AR, since radiation is a standard of care for locally advanced PCa where the AR is a major driver, and PARP inhibitors may be efficacious in CRPC patients with mutations in DDR genes (Polkinghorn et al., 2013; Goodwin et al., 2013; Ta et al., 2015; Mateo et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Radiation is a standard of care for locally advanced PCa where the AR is a major driver.
source: Recently, there has been an emphasis on understanding the link between the DDR and AR, since radiation is a standard of care for locally advanced PCa where the AR is a major driver
evidence: This claim is based on established medical knowledge and is supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of AR on S81 by CDK1 and CDK9 stimulates AR transcriptional activity and growth of PCa cells.
source: We focused on S81 and S308 phosphorylation since the phosphorylation of AR on S81 by CDK1 and CDK9 stimulates AR transcriptional activity and growth of PCa cells (Chen et al., 2006; Gordon et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AR phosphorylation on S308 by CDK1 represses AR transcriptional activity and alters AR localization during mitosis.
source: AR phosphorylation on S308 by CDK1 represses AR transcriptional activity and alters AR localization during mitosis (Gioeli et al., 2002; Zong et al., 2007).
